title: The Number Everyone Traded On Was Wrong by a Point
topics:
- macro
- policy
---

On October 29th, the first estimate said the economy grew 3.4% in the third quarter. This week the revision came in at 4.3%. That's nearly a full percentage point on a number the entire market treats as a fact the moment it prints. A friend of mine at the Times would call it a rounding error. I'd call it a rounding error the size of a mid-sized country's growth rate.

Trump's reaction is the part I keep rereading. He's calling the pre-midterm figures "fake" and demanding an investigation into a "record setting error." But the error ran in the direction of a weaker economy. The number that was too low is the one voters saw before they voted. Maybe there's a theory in there where that makes sense, though I can't find it from the headlines.

The market's reaction is stranger. CBS is asking why investors are "freaking out even as the economy surges," and the answer is sitting in the same week's news. The Fed has a hike pencilled in for December, and a hotter economy makes the pencil harder to erase. A 3.4% economy could plausibly absorb a pause. A 4.3% economy with CPI at 0.4% and wholesale prices up 6.5% year over year probably can't.

So the story isn't that the data got better. The Fed, bond traders and a few thousand analysts spent a month calibrating to a picture that was about a point too dim, and nobody had any way to know. How often does that happen, and how often does it go the other way?
